doc-0269dac08aa0d77a003eacc3c9780aae.content: {"feature": "NSP (Non-shareable policy (content should not be shared externally)) (Non-shareable policy (content should not be shared externally)) auto-flagging", "feature_description": "Automatically detect and tag content that violates NSP (Non-shareable policy (content should not be shared externally)) (content that should not be shared externally). When flagged, apply a Softblock (A user-level limitation applied silently without notifications) (a user-level limitation applied silently without notifications) and generate a Redline (Flag for legal review (different from its traditional business use for 'financial loss')) (flag for legal review) alert if downstream sharing is attempted.", "needs_geo_specific_logic": true, "reasoning": "Merged jury findings: U.S. federal law 18 U.S.C. §2258A creates a provider duty to report to NCMEC upon obtaining \"actual knowledge\" of facts or circumstances described in the statute (§2258A(a)(1)(A)(i)). The statute also enumerates the data elements that must be included in a report: historical reference (timestamps and provenance) (§2258A(a)(2)); geographic location information (IP address, verified address, or fallback identifiers such as area code/zip) (§2258A(a)(3)); any visual depictions of apparent child pornography (§2258A(a)(4)); and the complete communication including transmission metadata and attachments (§2258A(a)(5)). NCMEC, as clearinghouse, may forward reports to federal or certain foreign law enforcement (§2258A(c)) and law enforcement disclosure of report contents is tightly constrained (§2258A(g)). The statute also contains a privacy-protection clause stating providers are not required to monitor, scan, or affirmatively search (§2258A(f)), and prescribes civil penalties for knowing and willful failures to report (§2258A(b)(2)).\n\nOperational implications and conflict resolution: all jurors agreed geo-specific logic is required for US users. There is, however, an important legal/operational nuance: whether an automated model flag alone constitutes \"actual knowledge\" under §2258A is a legal threshold that requires counsel and clear internal policy. Product design must therefore treat automated detection as a potential trigger that requires defined verification and evidence-preservation workflows (human review or legally-authorized automated thresholds) before externally reporting. To minimize legal risk and satisfy the statute's data requirements, the feature must (a) route US-region detections through US reporting workflows (Geo-handler), (b) preserve original content and all transmission metadata, timestamps/timezones, and any available geographic identifiers, (c) capture provider contact information required by §2258A(a)(1)(B)(i), (d) log detection metadata (model outputs, confidence scores, who reviewed/when) to demonstrate good-faith processes and reduce risk of \"knowing and willful\" failure, and (e) ensure Softblock (A user-level limitation applied silently without notifications) behavior does not delete or irreversibly alter evidence prior to review/reporting. Jurors flagged an initial omission of the full subsection text in some materials; subsequent retrieved excerpts include §2258A(a)(1) language. Given remaining legal interpretation questions, product teams must obtain full statutory text, coordinate with legal counsel to define the internal threshold that converts an automated detection into reportable \"actual knowledge,\" and implement the evidence-preservation, routing, and escalation controls described above.
